title: The Free Son; the Fable That the Father Made the Son to Serve
english: … salvation and teaching to all: the true and free light, the Son. And he sets forth in a hidden way this truth, which some of them did not know because the memory of the polytheism of Egypt still rang in their ears.

So the august Son of God, bearing further witness that his own nature is free from above and does not have creation, so to speak, for a sister (for everything brought into being is the slave of the one who brought it into being, and what has been created is the creature of its creator), says to Peter: “From whom do the kings of the earth take toll or tribute? From their own sons, or from strangers?” And when he answered, “From strangers,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free. But so that we may not give them offence, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; when you open its mouth you will find a stater. Take that and give it to them for me and for you” (Matthew 17:25-27).
So much for these matters. Yet even so they do not stop.
On those who spin the fable that the Father made the Son for service in the work of creation.

Blasphemously they counter-attack and spin their fables, saying that the Father made for himself a Son, most useful for serving him in making the rest of the creatures. They no longer notice what hangs on this guesswork of theirs: envy, reluctance, and other things that belong to matter.

For surely these consequences too must be faced. If creating is good, as indeed it is good, and the sole property and sole prerogative of the divine and ungrudging nature, so that it might have someone by whom it is glorified, why did he not create all things through himself, but, as it were, shrank from the task? And if it is a great thing for created beings to be brought forward [...] by the greater and [...], if indeed, as they hold, the Father is greater than his own Son, the Word, did he begrudge those who glorify him the privilege of being made through himself?

And if making what is brought into being through a mediator is not altogether free at once of arrogance and of weakness, then it shows the glory of the one who brings a thing forth through himself to be greater than that of one who makes it through another. For what does not yet exist obeys the nod of him who always is: it is all but instantly brought to completion, receives its fitting measures, and lacks nothing in any part. [...] not only is the one who [...] arrogant, but already [...] would be shown [...] all that [...] authority and [...].

And if Jesus says to the dead Lazarus, “Come out!” (John 11:43), and to another, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Mark 2:5), and to another, “I command you: come out of him” (Mark 9:25), then for God to do these things through another, on their way of thinking, shows that God the Father, whose thought…
… of created gods, those who believe in the Son: this is what Paul, faithful to the law and made wise by the divine Spirit, guarantees.

More than that, he even calls “godless” those who before this knew God the Father alone, apart from the Son, since the Son is not counted among the things that were made. In one place he writes: “Remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called the uncircumcision by what is called the circumcision, made in the flesh by hand, were at that time without Christ, estranged from the hope of Israel and strangers to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and godless in the world” (Ephesians 2:11-12).

In another: “But then, when you did not know God, you were slaves to beings that by nature are not gods. Now, however, that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you want to be slaves all over again?” (Galatians 4:8-9).

Yet he holds the saving proclamation about Christ and the Holy Spirit, ever new and never sinking into old age, and the Church’s ordinance, to be more excellent than the older law, because it is perfect and has nothing either [...] lawless [...] to trouble it, or [...] finer or greater that ought to be set before it [...] in word or in manner [...]. For on this matter he writes to [...]: “I became”; “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to the righteousness that is in the law, blameless. But whatever gains I had, these I have counted loss for Christ’s sake. Indeed, I count all things to be loss because of the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as refuse, that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:6-8).
And to the Romans: “For if the one who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive” (2 Corinthians 11:4).

With what in view, then, and with what thoughts proper to a pure knowledge of God, has he written again? To the Corinthians, in the second letter, that if anyone is reconciled to the Son, he has been reconciled to God, and that the world’s accord with God is in Christ. title: The Father Whose Thoughts Are Deeds Needs No Helper
english: “… reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation. So we are ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were appealing through us. We plead on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:19-20).

And again, as though he had set everything else aside, he proclaimed with great boasting that even what seems to bring reproach on Christ, because of his loving dispensation for mankind, teems with all honour and strength. He does this, I think, on purpose, so that anyone who does not discern, from the glorious passion, the uncreated, pure and unchangeable Godhead may stand indicted for arrogance.

His words were these: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2). And to the Romans: “The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (Romans 3:22). Through faith in the Son, he says, each person is justified by God.

And to the Galatians: “Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Jesus Christ, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law; for by works of the law no flesh will be justified” (Galatians 2:16). And elsewhere too he explains that “neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

The saying runs deep, and its sense must be unfolded. What he means to teach is that the appearing of Christ found a new faith, the only faith, for all people, and by it left no room either for Judaism or for the religion of the Greeks. This faith may also be understood by the saying: “See, the old things have passed away; all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). And, to put it briefly [...], the one who knows God ceases from the law, since, he says, circumcision is not perfect.

But there shone forth for salvation and teaching to all the true and free light, the Son. And he sets forth in a hidden way this truth, which some of them did not know because the memory of the polytheism of Egypt still rang in their ears.

title: The Incomprehensibility of Divine Generation
english: … Son as a kind of lifeless instrument. How could anyone not spit hard at such savage slanders, hold up his upturned hands against them and withdraw, afraid of being held answerable before the divine court even for a hearing he did not choose?
On what the heretics say: “When was the Son begotten, and when did the Spirit proceed?” and the rest.

There are, then, so many and such clear proofs, and Scripture urges us “not to be carried away by various and strange teachings” (Hebrews 13:9) and to shun “empty talk” (2 Timothy 2:16). Yet the heterodox, at a loss to establish the tenets of their religion from the Scriptures, and [...] like drunken men, with their argument on each point tossed this way and that, put forward various sophisms, put together with evil craft and long rehearsed. Among them are these: “Are not all things, then,” he says, “from God?”

To them we must answer: Yes, but not by begetting, as the Son is, nor by procession, as the Spirit of God is; nor do they share in such operations, nor have they been counted worthy of so glorious a manner of existence.

Next: “When, then, was the Son begotten, and when did the Spirit proceed?” At the time when the Father was not begotten. For though they are from him, they are not after him. And as it is unlawful to seek [...] in a place, since neither the one who begot nor the one begotten is circumscribed [...], so neither [...] in time. For the Son, being God and the Word of the [...], [...] but of making. So too the Spirit [...].

“And how,” he says, “was he begotten?” It is written of the Son, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 110:3), and of the Holy Spirit, “A Spirit goes forth from me”; David sings, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6); Job says, “A divine Spirit is what made me, and the breath of the Almighty is what teaches me” (Job 33:4); the Lord teaches, “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26); and Paul writes that the Spirit is God’s own, as their own spirit is men’s (1 Corinthians 2:11). Yet even so, this so far surpasses every mind that the same Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us has made known the fragrance of the knowledge” (2 Corinthians 2:14). He means that, because it cannot be contained, we have not shared in the whole of the knowledge, but only, as it were, in a kind of semblance or waft of it.

And again: “We see through a mirror and in a riddle” (1 Corinthians 13:12) the things that concern him. And with good reason, for according to the divine saying, “The glory of the Lord hides a word” (Proverbs 25:2), since it lies beyond every created perception by a measure that is unspeakable and boundless. This is not only because it is too heavy to bear, but because what is before the ages and before all creation would have stayed unknown to creation had the Scriptures not made it known.

And again, writing a second time to the same readers, he puts it [...] most beautifully: “But we will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God has apportioned to us as a measure, to reach even as far as you” (2 Corinthians 10:13). And in the first letter he says: “If anyone thinks he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8:2).

What is the difference between begetting and procession? As the manner is unknown, so is the difference, if indeed it is permitted even to hear or to speak of this very thing. For to assign causes to what is beyond all cause and thought is rash; but to marvel at the divine, and to hold that the awesome thought of it is a thing to fear, is safe.

“Did God, then,” he says, “beget willingly or unwillingly?” But we must first state their aim and then answer. Their aim is to turn either word into a counter-argument against simple people. For if they seize on “he begot unwillingly” (though no one gives them that answer), they say: “Then God endured what he did not will when he begot the Son, the necessity of nature driving him to it against his will.” And if they are granted “he begot willingly”, they infer: “So the begetting of the Son hangs on the Father’s will, which gave him existence the way a maker does.”

But such an answer is utterly senseless. For both the God and Father who begot and “the radiance of his glory” (Hebrews 1:3), the Son, come before willing and not willing and before every concept; and nothing can be conceived between the Son and the one from whom he is. The same holds of “the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4). Again, the Son is an existence that neither begins nor ends, prior to willing or not willing. So he begot in the nature that is beyond counsel and mind.
But this premise of theirs too is full of absurdity. For a passion of desire goes before willing; and before not willing, yet making …

added_allusions.reason: “A Spirit goes forth from me” (πνεῦμα παρ’ ἐμοῦ ἐκπορεύεται) is close to the Greek (LXX) of Isaiah 57:16, πνεῦμα γὰρ παρ’ ἐμοῦ ἐξελεύσεται; the Hebrew and KJV read differently, so it is not cited inline.
The opponents’ question “Are not all things from God?” echoes τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ.
